0.title: The Lord Reigns over All
0.overview:
When Nebuchadnezzar, the most powerful king of his age, had been humbled by God and restored, he confessed something every human being needs to learn. God does according to his will among the host of heaven and among the inhabitants of the earth; and none can stay his hand or say to him, "What have you done?" (Dan 4:35). The emperor had discovered that he was not in charge. God was.

The sovereignty of God means that God is the supreme ruler of all things. He reigns over creation, over history, over nations and kings, over the smallest details of life, over good and even over evil, and over the salvation of sinners. Nothing happens outside his knowledge, his power or his purpose. Our God is in the heavens; he does all that he pleases (Ps 115:3).

For some, this truth is troubling. It raises hard questions about evil, suffering and human freedom. Those questions are real, and this study does not avoid them. But for God's people, his sovereignty is first of all a comfort. It means that the world is not out of control, that our lives are not ruled by chance, that evil will not have the last word, and that God's promises cannot fail. My times are in your hand (Ps 31:15).

This study follows the historic Reformed understanding of God's sovereignty, which holds that God ordains whatever comes to pass, yet is never the author of sin, and that human beings make real choices for which they are responsible. Where Christians differ, especially on election, the main views are explained fairly before a conclusion is given.

Six units: (1) What It Means That God Is Sovereign; (2) Sovereign over Creation and Providence; (3) Sovereign over History, Nations and Evil; (4) Sovereign in Salvation; (5) Sovereignty and Human Responsibility; (6) Living Under a Sovereign God. It belongs with the studies on the Holiness of God, the Grace of God and the Fear of the Lord.

1.title: What It Means That God Is Sovereign
1.overview:
To say that God is sovereign is to say that he is King, absolutely. The LORD has established his throne in the heavens, and his kingdom rules over all (Ps 103:19). His rule has no boundaries, no rivals and no end.

Scripture describes God's sovereignty in several ways. He has all authority: he is the blessed and only Sovereign, the King of kings and Lord of lords (1 Tim 6:15). He has all power: Nothing is too hard for you (Jer 32:17). He has a plan that cannot fail: declaring the end from the beginning and from ancient times things not yet done, saying, 'My counsel shall stand, and I will accomplish all my purpose' (Isa 46:10). And his plan includes everything: he works all things according to the counsel of his will (Eph 1:11).

Notice the words "all things." God's sovereignty is not limited to the big events of history while the details are left to chance. Nor is it a power he holds in reserve and rarely uses. It is his active, ongoing rule over every part of his creation.

And this sovereign God is not a cold force or an impersonal fate. He is the God revealed in Scripture: holy, wise, just and good. His sovereignty is the sovereignty of a Father who knows the number of hairs on his children's heads. It is exercised by a King who wept at a grave and died on a cross. When we speak of God's sovereignty, we are not speaking of raw power but of the rule of the God of love.

Job, after all his questions, came to this conclusion: I know that you can do all things, and that no purpose of yours can be thwarted (Job 42:2). It did not answer every question, but it brought him peace.
1.theology:
Not fate: Some think God's sovereignty is the same as fatalism, the idea that impersonal forces determine everything and our choices do not matter. Scripture's teaching is entirely different. Fate is blind; God is wise and good. Fate makes choices meaningless; God works through human choices, and they matter (unit 5).

Not tyranny: A human ruler with absolute power is dangerous, because human beings are sinful. God's absolute power is safe, because he is perfectly holy and good. for all his works are right and his ways are just (Dan 4:37).

Not only permission: Some speak as if God merely permits events he does not control. Scripture goes further. God does not just watch history; he directs it. Even when he permits evil, he does so with purpose, and he limits it and turns it to good (Gen 50:20).

God's will in two senses: Scripture speaks of God's will in two ways. His will of command tells us what we ought to do (for example, do not steal). His will of decree is his plan for everything that happens. People often break God's commands, but no one can frustrate his decree. The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us (Deut 29:29). We are to live by what he has revealed and trust him with what he has not.
1.examples:
Then: Nebuchadnezzar looked over Babylon and said, in effect, "I built this by my power for my glory" (Dan 4:30). God humbled him for seven periods of time until he learned that the Most High rules the kingdom of men (Dan 4:32). When his reason returned, he praised God's everlasting dominion. The most powerful man in the world had to learn he was not sovereign.

Now: A business owner who has always prided himself on being in control loses a major contract through no fault of his own. For the first time he realizes how little he controls. It is frightening at first. Then, through a friend at church, he begins to see that someone else is in control, and that this someone is good. His anxiety slowly turns into trust.

A simple test: When things go wrong, which thought comes first: "Everything is falling apart," or "God is still on the throne"? The second does not remove pain, but it changes everything about how we carry it.

verseByVerse.quote: Our God is in the heavens; he does all that he pleases. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This verse is set in a contrast. The nations mock Israel: Where is their God? (Ps 115:2). The psalmist answers that Israel's God is in the heavens, doing all he pleases, while the nations' idols have mouths that cannot speak and hands that cannot act (Ps 115:4-8). A god who cannot act is no god. The true God is free, powerful and active. And because he does all that he pleases, and what pleases him is always right, his people can trust him completely.

verseByVerse.quote: remember the former things of old; for I am God, and there is no other; I am God, and there is none like me, declaring the end from the beginning and from ancient times things not yet done, saying, 'My counsel shall stand, and I will accomplish all my purpose,' (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God challenges the idols of Babylon by pointing to one thing only he can do: declaring the end from the beginning. He not only knows the future; he has planned it, and he will bring it to pass. My counsel shall stand, and I will accomplish all my purpose. This was spoken to exiles who felt their history had collapsed. God's answer was not "I am sorry things went wrong" but "Nothing has gone outside my plan." That is the comfort of his sovereignty.

verseByVerse.quote: In him we have obtained an inheritance, having been predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's phrase is sweeping: God works all things according to the counsel of his will. Not some things, not most things, but all things. And notice the setting. Paul is not writing a philosophical argument; he is praising God for salvation. Our inheritance in Christ is secure because it rests on the purpose of the God who works everything according to his plan. The sovereignty of God is not a cold doctrine but a warm assurance for believers.

verseByVerse.quote: At the end of the days I, Nebuchadnezzar, lifted my eyes to heaven, and my reason returned to me, and I blessed the Most High, and praised and honored him who lives forever, for his dominion is an everlasting dominion, and his kingdom endures from generation to generation; all the inhabitants of the earth are accounted as nothing, and he does according to his will among the host of heaven and among the inhabitants of the earth; and none can stay his hand or say to him, "What have you done?" (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: These are the words of a pagan king who had been humbled by God. He confesses that God's dominion is an everlasting dominion, that the inhabitants of the earth are accounted as nothing before him, and that none can stay his hand. This is a remarkable testimony: the most powerful ruler on earth acknowledging a higher throne. Every human ruler, every government and every powerful person will one day have to make the same confession.

1.reflection:
Before this study, how would you have defined the sovereignty of God? What would you add now?

How is God's sovereignty different from fate? Why does that difference matter?

Read Isaiah 46:8-11. How would these words have comforted exiles in Babylon? How do they comfort you?

Where in your life are you most tempted to think things are out of control?

2.title: Sovereign over Creation and Providence
2.overview:
God did not create the world and then leave it to run on its own. He made it, and he continues to uphold and govern it every moment. Theologians call this providence: God's ongoing care and control of all his creatures and all their actions.

Christ himself upholds the universe by the word of his power (Heb 1:3). He is before all things, and in him all things hold together (Col 1:17). If God withdrew his sustaining power for a moment, the universe would not continue.

And God's providence reaches the smallest details. Jesus said, Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? And not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your Father. But even the hairs of your head are all numbered (Matt 10:29-30). A sparrow was among the cheapest things in the market. Yet not one falls apart from the Father. Proverbs says, The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD (Prov 16:33). Even what looks like chance is under God's hand.

God's providence also governs our lives. Your eyes saw my unformed substance; in your book were written, every one of them, the days that were formed for me, when as yet there was none of them (Ps 139:16). Where we were born, the families we belong to and the length of our lives are all in his hands. Paul told the Athenians that God made from one man every nation of mankind to live on all the face of the earth, having determined allotted periods and the boundaries of their dwelling place (Acts 17:26).

This means there is no such thing as luck for a Christian. There are only the purposes of a wise and loving Father, some of which we see and many of which we do not.
2.theology:
Preservation and government: Providence includes God's preservation of all things, keeping them in existence, and his government of all things, directing them to his purposes. he himself gives to all mankind life and breath and everything (Acts 17:25).

Ordinary means: God usually works through ordinary means: weather, medicine, work, human decisions. Providence does not make these unimportant. It means God is at work in them. A Christian takes medicine and prays, plants seed and thanks God for the harvest.

Christ at the centre: Colossians says that all things were created through him and for him (Col 1:16). The Son who upholds the universe is the Son who died for sinners. The hands that hold the world together are the hands that were pierced.

Good and hard providences: Job, after losing everything, said, The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD (Job 1:21). He did not blame chance or Satan alone. He saw God's hand in both blessing and loss, and he worshipped.
2.examples:
Then: Ruth went out to glean grain, and she happened to come to the part of the field belonging to Boaz (Ruth 2:3). The narrator says "happened" with a smile. From Ruth's point of view it was chance. From God's point of view it was the first step toward a marriage that would lead to King David and, in time, to Christ (Matt 1:5). The book of Ruth is a quiet lesson in providence.

Then: In Jonah the LORD appointed a great fish (Jonah 1:17), a plant (Jonah 4:6), a worm and a wind (Jonah 4:7-8). Fish, plants, worms and weather are all at God's command, serving his purpose to teach a stubborn prophet.

Now: A young woman misses a train and, waiting for the next one, sits beside someone who later becomes her husband. A man loses a job, and the job he finds next puts him in a church where he hears the gospel. Looking back, both see what they could not see at the time: God was arranging the details.

Now: A Christian facing surgery prays, trusts God and is grateful for skilled doctors. She does not see medicine and providence as rivals. God works through the surgeon's hands.

verseByVerse.quote: Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? And not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your Father. But even the hairs of your head are all numbered. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus chose the smallest, cheapest example he could find. Two sparrows for a penny. If God's care reaches a sparrow, how much more his children. And then even smaller: the hairs of your head. No one knows how many hairs they have. God does, because he knows everything about us. The point of this verse is not to make us anxious but to free us from anxiety. Jesus goes on, Fear not, therefore; you are of more value than many sparrows (Matt 10:31).

verseByVerse.quote: He is the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature, and he upholds the universe by the word of his power. After making purification for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The writer describes the Son of God in majestic terms, and in the middle of the description is this: he upholds the universe by the word of his power. The universe does not hold itself together. Christ holds it, constantly, by his word. And in the same verse: After making purification for sins, he sat down. The one who sustains galaxies is the one who died for our sins. His power is in the service of his grace.

verseByVerse.quote: The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: In Israel, casting lots was a common way to make decisions, something like rolling dice. It seems the very definition of chance. Yet Proverbs says that its every decision is from the LORD. Nothing is truly random. This does not mean Christians should make decisions by drawing lots today; we have God's word and the Spirit's wisdom. But it does mean that even the events that look most accidental are under God's hand.

verseByVerse.quote: Your eyes saw my unformed substance; in your book were written, every one of them, the days that were formed for me, when as yet there was none of them. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: David marvels that God knew him before he was born. God saw his unformed substance in the womb, and all his days were written in God's book before one of them had happened. This is not a cold record but a loving plan. Every day of our lives, including the days we would not have chosen, has been seen and ordained by a God who knit us together. Our lives are not accidents. They are written by a loving author.

2.reflection:
Read Ruth 2. Where do you see God's providence at work in "chance" events?

Look back over your life. What "accidents" do you now see as God's providence?

How does Matthew 10:29-31 speak to your anxieties?

Job blessed God's name in loss as well as gain (Job 1:21). What would that look like for you right now?

3.title: Sovereign over History, Nations and Evil
3.overview:
God's sovereignty extends to the rise and fall of nations and the decisions of the powerful. He changes times and seasons; he removes kings and sets up kings (Dan 2:21). The king's heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD; he turns it wherever he will (Prov 21:1). Rulers plan and scheme, but The counsel of the LORD stands forever, the plans of his heart to all generations (Ps 33:11).

God even raises up unbelieving rulers to carry out his purposes. He called Cyrus, the Persian king, his anointed, and used him to return the exiles to Jerusalem (Isa 45:1). He used Assyria as the rod of my anger against Israel (Isa 10:5), even though Assyria had no intention of serving God: But he does not so intend, and his heart does not so think (Isa 10:7). Assyria meant destruction; God meant discipline. And afterwards God judged Assyria for its pride and cruelty (Isa 10:12).

That raises the hardest question: how does God's sovereignty relate to evil? Scripture holds two truths together. First, God is sovereign even over evil acts. The clearest example is the cross. this Jesus, delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men (Acts 2:23). The greatest crime in history was within God's plan. Second, God is never the author of sin, and those who do evil are fully responsible. Let no one say when he is tempted, "I am being tempted by God," for God cannot be tempted with evil, and he himself tempts no one (Jas 1:13). The men who crucified Jesus were lawless, and they were guilty.

How both can be true, we cannot fully explain. But Scripture insists on both, and we see them together in Joseph's words to his brothers: you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Gen 50:20). The same event had two purposes: the brothers' evil purpose and God's good one. God did not make them sin. But he ruled over their sin and turned it to salvation.
3.theology:
God is not the author of sin: The Reformed confessions are careful here. God ordains all that happens, yet he does not do evil, approve evil or force anyone to sin. Evil comes from the wicked desires of creatures (Jas 1:14). God's sovereignty over evil means he restrains it, limits it, judges it and overrules it for good.

The cross is the proof: If God could take the murder of his own Son, carried out by wicked men, and make it the salvation of the world, then he can rule over every lesser evil. to do whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place (Acts 4:28).

Evil will not win: Why do the nations rage and the peoples plot in vain? (Ps 2:1). The rulers of the earth set themselves against God and his Anointed, and He who sits in the heavens laughs (Ps 2:4). Every rebellion against God is ultimately futile.

Mystery and trust: We should not pretend to understand more than we do. Paul, after wrestling with God's sovereignty in Romans 9-11, does not end with a neat explanation but with worship: How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways! (Rom 11:33).
3.examples:
Then: Joseph's brothers sold him into slavery out of jealousy. He was falsely accused and imprisoned for years. But when he finally met them again, he said, God sent me before you to preserve life (Gen 45:5), and later, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Gen 50:20). He did not excuse their sin. But he saw God's hand above it.

Then: Pilate told Jesus he had authority to release him or crucify him. Jesus answered, You would have no authority over me at all unless it had been given you from above (John 19:11). The Roman governor thought he was in control. He was not.

Now: A Christian who was abused as a child struggles with the idea of God's sovereignty. "How could God allow it?" Wise counsel does not give quick answers. It affirms that what was done to her was evil and that God hates it. It points her to the cross, where God brought good out of the worst evil, and to the promise that God will judge every wrong. In time, she may come to say with Joseph that what others meant for evil, God is turning for good, without ever calling the evil good.

Now: Christians in a country where the government is hostile to the church are tempted to despair. Psalm 2 and Daniel remind them that God sets up and removes rulers, and that no regime is beyond his reach.

verseByVerse.quote: But Joseph said to them, "Do not fear, for am I in the place of God? As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive, as they are today. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Joseph's brothers feared revenge after their father's death. Joseph's answer begins with humility: am I in the place of God? He will not take God's role as judge. Then he gives one of the clearest statements of providence in the Bible. The same act, selling him into slavery, had two intentions. you meant evil; God meant it for good. The brothers were responsible for their evil. God was sovereign over it and used it to save many lives. That is how God's sovereignty and human sin relate.

verseByVerse.quote: this Jesus, delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Peter's sermon at Pentecost holds two truths in one sentence. Jesus was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God. And you crucified and killed him by the hands of lawless men. God planned it; men did it; and the men were guilty. Peter does not explain how both are true. He proclaims both, and then calls his hearers to repent (Acts 2:38). God's sovereignty never removes human guilt.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to Assyria, the rod of my anger; the staff in their hands is my fury! Against a godless nation I send him, and against the people of my wrath I command him, to take spoil and seize plunder, and to tread them down like the mire of the streets. But he does not so intend, and his heart does not so think; but it is in his heart to destroy, and to cut off nations not a few; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God calls Assyria the rod of my anger. He used this cruel empire to discipline his unfaithful people. But Assyria had no idea it was serving God. he does not so intend, and his heart does not so think. Assyria was simply greedy for conquest. God used its ambition for his own just purposes, and then judged it for its arrogance (Isa 10:12-15). Nations and rulers who think they are acting entirely on their own are, without knowing it, instruments in God's hand.

verseByVerse.quote: The king's heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD; he turns it wherever he will. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: In the ancient world, a king's word was law, and his heart seemed the most independent thing on earth. Yet Proverbs says that even the king's heart is like water in an irrigation channel, which the farmer directs wherever he wants. God can turn the heart of the most powerful ruler. This is a great encouragement to pray for those in authority (1 Tim 2:1-2). No president, prime minister or dictator is beyond God's reach.

3.reflection:
Read Genesis 50:15-21. How does Joseph hold together human sin and God's sovereignty?

Why is it important to affirm both that God is sovereign over evil and that he is never the author of sin?

How does the cross (Acts 2:23; 4:27-28) help you trust God's sovereignty in your own suffering?

Which ruler or nation do you need to pray for, trusting that "the king's heart is ... in the hand of the LORD"?

4.title: Sovereign in Salvation
4.overview:
The Bible teaches that God is sovereign not only over creation and history but over salvation. Paul begins Ephesians with a song of praise for it: even as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him. In love he predestined us for adoption to himself as sons through Jesus Christ, according to the purpose of his will (Eph 1:4-5).

Scripture uses several words for this. God chose or elected his people. He predestined them. He foreknew them, which in Scripture means more than knowing facts about them in advance; it means setting his love on them beforehand (Rom 8:29). And from that choice flows the whole chain of salvation: those whom he predestined he also called, and those whom he called he also justified, and those whom he justified he also glorified (Rom 8:30). Not one link breaks.

Why does God choose some? Paul's answer is not something in us, but God's mercy: I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion. So then it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who has mercy (Rom 9:15-16). Jesus thanked his Father for the same truth: you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children; yes, Father, for such was your gracious will (Matt 11:25-26).

This doctrine is meant to humble us and to comfort us. It humbles us because it leaves no room for boasting: we did not choose God first; he chose us. And it comforts us because a salvation that rests on God's choice is secure. If it depended on us, we could lose it. Because it depends on him, it cannot fail.
4.theology:
Two views of election: Christians understand election in two main ways. The Arminian view holds that God chose those whom he foresaw would believe: election is conditional on foreseen faith. The Reformed view holds that God chose his people unconditionally, not because of anything he foresaw in them, and that faith is the result of election, not its cause. Both views affirm that the gospel should be preached to all and that everyone who believes will be saved. The Reformed view is the more likely reading of Scripture. Paul grounds election in God's purpose not because of our works but because of his own purpose and grace (2 Tim 1:9); he says it depends not on human will or exertion (Rom 9:16); and Luke writes that as many as were appointed to eternal life believed (Acts 13:48), not the reverse. If election were based on foreseen faith, it would finally depend on us, and Paul's careful denial of that would make no sense.

Election in Christ: God chose us in him (Eph 1:4). Election is never apart from Christ. We should not look for assurance of election in secret decrees but in Christ, trusting him as he is offered in the gospel.

Election and holiness: God chose us that we should be holy and blameless before him (Eph 1:4). Election is not a licence for careless living. It is the root of a holy life.

Election and evangelism: Paul said, Therefore I endure everything for the sake of the elect, that they also may obtain the salvation (2 Tim 2:10). Election did not make Paul passive. It made him confident that his preaching would bear fruit.
4.examples:
Then: In Corinth Paul faced opposition and may have been tempted to leave. The Lord said to him, Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent, for I am with you ... for I have many in this city who are my people (Acts 18:9-10). They were not yet believers, but they were God's. Paul stayed a year and a half, preaching, and they came to faith.

Now: A young believer struggles with election. "What if I am not chosen?" A wise pastor answers that the question is not where to start. Start with Christ, who says, whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37). If you have come to him, trusting him, that is the evidence that God has drawn you. Election is not a barrier to coming; it is the reason anyone comes at all.

Now: A missionary works for years in a hard field with little fruit. Election gives her confidence: God has his people there, and his word will not return empty (Isa 55:11). She keeps preaching, praying and loving, trusting the Lord of the harvest.

verseByVerse.quote: even as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him. In love he predestined us for adoption to himself as sons through Jesus Christ, according to the purpose of his will, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul is not arguing here; he is worshipping. Election comes at the start of a long sentence of praise (Eph 1:3-14). God chose us before the foundation of the world, before we had done anything good or bad. He chose us in him, in Christ. He chose us for a purpose: to be holy. And he chose us In love, predestining us for adoption. Election is not a cold decree but the love of a Father who planned to bring us into his family before time began.

verseByVerse.quote: For he says to Moses, "I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion." So then it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who has mercy. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul quotes God's words to Moses: I will have mercy on whom I have mercy. Mercy, by definition, is not owed. If God gave it to everyone automatically, it would not be mercy. And Paul draws the conclusion: salvation depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who has mercy. This is humbling. But it is also hopeful. If salvation depended on human will, no one would be saved. Because it depends on God's mercy, even the hardest sinner may be saved.

verseByVerse.quote: And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose. For those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, in order that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. And those whom he predestined he also called, and those whom he called he also justified, and those whom he justified he also glorified. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Verse 28 is one of the most loved verses in the Bible, and verses 29-30 explain why it is true. All things work together for good for God's people because God has a purpose for them that runs from eternity past to eternity future: foreknown, predestined, called, justified, glorified. Paul even writes "glorified" in the past tense, because it is as certain as if it had already happened. Nothing in between, no suffering, no failure, no enemy, can break the chain.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time Jesus declared, "I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children; yes, Father, for such was your gracious will. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus rejoices that the Father has hidden the truth from the proud and revealed it to little children. And he gives the reason: for such was your gracious will. Jesus did not find God's sovereign choice troubling. He found it a reason for thanksgiving. The Father does not save people because they are clever or impressive. He saves the humble, and he does it graciously. The right response to election is not argument but praise.

4.reflection:
How does Ephesians 1:3-14 present election: as a problem or as a reason for praise?

Why does it matter whether election is based on God's choice or on our foreseen faith?

How would you answer a friend who worries, "What if I am not chosen?"

How should election shape the way you pray for and share the gospel with others?

5.title: Sovereignty and Human Responsibility
5.overview:
If God ordains all things, do our choices matter? Scripture's answer is a clear yes. God's sovereignty and human responsibility are both true, and the Bible teaches both without embarrassment.

Look at Paul in the storm (Acts 27). An angel told him that God had granted you all those who sail with you (Acts 27:24). Everyone's survival was certain. Yet when some sailors tried to escape in the lifeboat, Paul said, Unless these men stay in the ship, you cannot be saved (Acts 27:31). God had promised the result, and he would bring it about through the sailors staying and working. God's sovereignty did not make their actions unnecessary. It included them.

The same pattern runs through Scripture. The heart of man plans his way, but the LORD establishes his steps (Prov 16:9). We plan; God directs. Paul tells believers, work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure (Phil 2:12-13). We work because God works. His work does not cancel ours; it makes ours possible.

This truth guards against two errors. The first is fatalism: "If God has decided everything, nothing I do matters." Scripture says our choices are real and we will give account for them. The second is self-reliance: "Everything depends on me." Scripture says God is the one who brings our efforts to their result. The biblical attitude is to work as hard as we can, pray as though everything depends on God, and rest because it does.

James gives a practical example. He rebukes people who plan their business trips as though they controlled the future. Instead you ought to say, "If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that." (Jas 4:15). Planning is not wrong. Planning without God is.
5.theology:
Compatibility: Reformed theology teaches that God's sovereignty and human responsibility are compatible. God ordains what happens, and humans freely choose according to their desires. We are not robots. We do what we want to do, and we are responsible for it. Yet God is sovereign over our wants and our choices. How he does this is beyond our understanding, but both truths are clearly taught.

Prayer matters: Some ask why we should pray if God has already decided everything. Scripture's answer is that God has ordained to work through prayer. Prayer is one of the means by which God accomplishes his purposes. Jesus, who knew his Father's plan perfectly, prayed constantly.

Evangelism matters: God's sovereign election does not make evangelism unnecessary. It makes it hopeful. God saves people through the preaching of the gospel (Rom 10:14-17). Because he has his people everywhere, we can preach with confidence.

Responsibility for sin: No one will be able to blame God for their sin. But who are you, O man, to answer back to God? (Rom 9:20). Paul does not give a philosophical answer to every objection. He reminds us that the creature does not sit in judgment on the Creator.
5.examples:
Then: Esther was in the right place at the right time, as queen of Persia when her people faced extermination. Mordecai told her that God's deliverance would come regardless: relief and deliverance will rise for the Jews from another place. But he also urged her to act: And who knows whether you have not come to the kingdom for such a time as this? (Esth 4:14). God's sovereignty was the reason for her courage, not an excuse for inaction.

Now: A student facing important exams says, "God is sovereign, so I don't need to study." That is fatalism, not faith. Another student is so anxious that she cannot sleep, as if everything depends on her. That is self-reliance. The biblical way is to study diligently, pray honestly, and sleep peacefully, trusting God with the result.

Now: A church is planning a new outreach. Some members say, "If God wants people saved, he will save them; we don't need to plan." Others act as if success depends entirely on good strategy. The elders lead them to plan carefully, pray earnestly and depend on God for the fruit.

Now: A father plans a family move for a new job, saying, "If the Lord wills, we will go." When the job falls through, he is disappointed but not crushed. He trusts that God's plan for his family is better than his own.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet now I urge you to take heart, for there will be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship. For this very night there stood before me an angel of the God to whom I belong and whom I worship, and he said, 'Do not be afraid, Paul; you must stand before Caesar. And behold, God has granted you all those who sail with you.' So take heart, men, for I have faith in God that it will be exactly as I have been told. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: In the middle of a terrifying storm, Paul received a promise from God: no one on board would die. And he believed it: I have faith in God that it will be exactly as I have been told. But a few verses later he insisted that the sailors must stay on the ship and everyone must eat (Acts 27:31-34). Paul saw no contradiction. God's promise was certain, and God would fulfil it through ordinary human action. Faith in God's sovereignty made Paul calm and practical, not passive.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, my beloved, as you have always obeyed, so now, not only as in my presence but much more in my absence, work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul tells the Philippians to work out their salvation, to put it into practice with serious effort. And the reason is not "because it all depends on you" but for it is God who works in you. God works in us both to will, giving us the desire, and to work, giving us the ability. Our effort is real, and it is the fruit of his work. The more we understand that God is at work in us, the more energetically we should work.

verseByVerse.quote: The heart of man plans his way, but the LORD establishes his steps. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This proverb affirms both sides. The heart of man plans his way: planning is good and right. But the LORD establishes his steps: God determines the outcome. We are responsible to plan wisely, and we are to hold our plans with an open hand. Many believers can look back and see how God redirected their steps, closing doors they wanted open and opening doors they never expected. His direction was better than their plans.

verseByVerse.quote: Come now, you who say, "Today or tomorrow we will go into such and such a town and spend a year there and trade and make a profit"— yet you do not know what tomorrow will bring. What is your life? For you are a mist that appears for a little time and then vanishes. Instead you ought to say, "If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: James is not against business, travel or planning. He is against presumption, planning as though we controlled tomorrow. you do not know what tomorrow will bring. Life is a mist. And so the Christian way is to say, If the Lord wills. This is not a superstitious phrase to add to sentences. It is a posture of the heart, a humble acknowledgement that our lives and plans are in God's hands.

5.reflection:
Read Acts 27. How did Paul combine trust in God's promise with practical action?

Are you more prone to fatalism ("nothing I do matters") or to self-reliance ("everything depends on me")?

Why should God's sovereignty make us more, not less, committed to prayer and evangelism?

What plans do you need to hold with an open hand, saying "If the Lord wills"?

6.title: Living Under a Sovereign God
6.overview:
The sovereignty of God is not only a doctrine to believe. It is a truth to live by, and it transforms how we face every part of life.

It gives comfort in suffering. And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose (Rom 8:28). Not all things are good. But God works all things together for good for his people. Nothing is wasted.

It gives peace in anxiety. Jesus told his disciples not to worry about food or clothing, because your heavenly Father knows that you need them all (Matt 6:32). Anxiety often comes from feeling that everything depends on us. It does not. Be still, and know that I am God (Ps 46:10).

It gives courage in danger. If God is sovereign, then no enemy can touch us except by his permission, and no enemy can finally harm us. The early Christians, threatened by the authorities, prayed to God as Sovereign Lord, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and everything in them (Acts 4:24), and then spoke the word with boldness.

It gives humility in success. Both riches and honor come from you, and you rule over all (1 Chr 29:12). Whatever we achieve is a gift. There is no room for pride.

It gives hope for the future. History is not going nowhere. It is heading toward the day when the great multitude will cry, Hallelujah! For the Lord our God the Almighty reigns (Rev 19:6). God's purposes will be fulfilled, his kingdom will come, and every knee will bow.

And it leads to worship. Paul ends his long discussion of God's sovereign purposes not with an argument but with a doxology: For from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory forever. Amen. (Rom 11:36).
6.theology:
All things for good: Romans 8:28 does not promise that believers will escape suffering. Romans 8 goes on to speak of tribulation, distress, persecution and death (Rom 8:35-36). The promise is that none of these will be wasted, and none can separate us from the love of God in Christ.

Light and momentary: Paul, who suffered greatly, could write, For this light momentary affliction is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison (2 Cor 4:17). God's sovereignty gives our suffering eternal significance.

God's ways are higher: For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways and my thoughts than your thoughts (Isa 55:9). We will not always understand what God is doing. Trust does not require understanding. It requires knowing who God is.

The throne is occupied: In Revelation 4, before the seals, trumpets and bowls of judgment, John sees a throne in heaven, and someone seated on it. Whatever happens on earth, the throne of heaven is occupied, and the one who sits there is worthy of all worship (Rev 4:11).
6.examples:
Then: When Peter and John were threatened by the authorities, the church did not panic. They prayed, quoting Psalm 2, and acknowledging that their enemies had done only whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place (Acts 4:28). Then they asked not for safety but for boldness, and they received it (Acts 4:29-31).

Now: A family receives a frightening medical diagnosis. They are grieved and afraid. But they pray together, read Psalm 46 and Romans 8, and find that the sovereignty of God holds them up. They do not know the outcome. They know who holds it.

Now: A successful businesswoman is praised at an awards ceremony. In her short speech she thanks her team, and then simply says that every gift she has comes from God. Her colleagues notice. Her humility in success is a witness.

Now: An elderly believer, watching the world grow darker, refuses to despair. "I have read the end of the book," he says. "The Lord our God the Almighty reigns."

This week: Read Psalm 46 each morning. When anxiety rises, say, "Be still, and know that I am God." Thank God for one providence in your past. Add "If the Lord wills" to your plans, and mean it.

verseByVerse.quote: And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This promise is for those who love God, those who are called according to his purpose. It is not a general statement that everything turns out well for everyone. It is a family promise. And it does not say that all things are good. Cancer, betrayal and grief are not good. It says that God works all things together for good. Like a skilled weaver who uses dark threads as well as bright ones, God weaves every event into a pattern of good for his people. And the good is defined in the next verse: being conformed to the image of his Son (Rom 8:29).

verseByVerse.quote: "Be still, and know that I am God. I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted in the earth!" (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Psalm 46 is set in a world of chaos: mountains falling into the sea, nations raging, kingdoms tottering. And in the middle of it, God speaks: Be still, and know that I am God. The command is not first a call to quiet meditation, though it includes that. It is a call to stop striving, to stop fighting and fretting, and to recognize who is in control. I will be exalted among the nations. Whatever is happening, God's purposes will prevail.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways! "For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?" "Or who has given a gift to him that he might be repaid?" For from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory forever. Amen. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: After three chapters on God's sovereign purposes for Israel and the nations, Paul does not conclude with a tidy explanation. He bursts into praise. God's wisdom is deep; his judgments are unsearchable; no one has been his counsellor; no one has given him anything he must repay. For from him and through him and to him are all things. Everything comes from God, is sustained by God and exists for God. The right response to God's sovereignty is not anxiety or argument, but worship.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I heard what seemed to be the voice of a great multitude, like the roar of many waters and like the sound of mighty peals of thunder, crying out, "Hallelujah! For the Lord our God the Almighty reigns. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This is the song of heaven at the end of history. Babylon has fallen; evil has been judged; the marriage of the Lamb has come. And the great multitude cries out: Hallelujah! For the Lord our God the Almighty reigns. He reigned all along, even when it did not look like it. Now everyone will see it. Christians can sing this song already, by faith, in the middle of a world that does not yet see it.

6.reflection:
Read Romans 8:28-39. How does God's sovereignty give you comfort in your current circumstances?

Which area of your life most needs the word "Be still, and know that I am God"?

How should God's sovereignty shape the way you respond to success?

Write your own short prayer of praise to the sovereign God, using Romans 11:33-36 as a model.
